title: Book 2 — Euterpe, Chapter 356
paragraphs: After him the priest of Hephaistos, whose name was Sethos, came to the throne. This man, they said, neglected and held in no regard the warrior class of the Egyptians, thinking he would have no need of them. Besides other slights he put upon them, he also took from them the plots of grain-land which had been granted to them as a special gift in the reigns of previous kings — twelve plots to each man. After this, Sanacharib, king of the Arabians and Assyrians, marched a great army against Egypt. Then the warriors of the Egyptians refused to come to the rescue, and the priest, being driven into a tight corner, entered the sanctuary of the temple and lamented before the image of the god the danger hanging over him. As he was lamenting, sleep came over him, and in his vision it seemed that the god came and stood beside him and encouraged him, saying he would suffer no harm if he went out to meet the army of the Arabians, for he himself would send him helpers. Trusting in what he had seen in his sleep, he took with him, they said, those Egyptians who were willing to follow, and encamped at Pelusion, for that was the route of the invasion. Not one of the warrior class followed him, but shopkeepers, artisans, and men of the marketplace. Then, after they arrived, field mice swarmed by night upon their enemies and ate through their quivers and their bows, and moreover the handgrips of their shields, so that the next day they fled, and being without weapons to defend themselves, great numbers of them fell. To this day this king stands in the temple of Hephaistos in stone, holding a mouse on his hand, and by letters inscribed he says these words: “Let whoever looks upon me learn to fear the gods.”
